Kappa and finite-sample concentration

How much does averaging reduce mean absolute error at a specified sample size? Kappa records the growth of the sum’s absolute deviation between two sizes. It depends on the whole distribution and the chosen sizes. A tail exponent alone does not determine it.

We use the metric from Taleb (2025), ch. 8, §§8.1–8.3, pp. 154–160. The derivations below establish the stated special cases and corrections; simulated values are labeled separately. The chapter guide maps the remaining source sections.

Definition and domain¶

Let XiX_iXi​ be iid, with E∣X1∣<∞\mathbb E|X_1|<\inftyE∣X1​∣<∞, mean μ\muμ, and sums Sn=∑i=1nXiS_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_iSn​=∑i=1n​Xi​, as in the shared notation. Define

M(n)=E∣Sn−nμ∣,E∣Xˉn−μ∣=M(n)/n.\begin{aligned} M(n)&=\mathbb E|S_n-n\mu|,\\ \mathbb E|\bar X_n-\mu|&=M(n)/n. \end{aligned}M(n)E∣Xˉn​−μ∣​=E∣Sn​−nμ∣,=M(n)/n.​
(1)

MMM is a mean absolute deviation about the population mean, without Gaussian calibration. It is neither a median deviation nor a deviation about an estimated center; see the dispersion note. For integers n>n0≥1n>n_0\ge1n>n0​≥1, with M(n)>M(n0)>0M(n)>M(n_0)>0M(n)>M(n0​)>0, set

κn0,n=2−log⁡(n/n0)log⁡(M(n)/M(n0)),M(n)M(n0)=(n/n0)1/(2−κn0,n).\begin{aligned} \kappa_{n_0,n} &=2-\frac{\log(n/n_0)}{\log(M(n)/M(n_0))},\\ \frac{M(n)}{M(n_0)} &=(n/n_0)^{1/(2-\kappa_{n_0,n})}. \end{aligned}κn0​,n​M(n0​)M(n)​​=2−log(M(n)/M(n0​))log(n/n0​)​,=(n/n0​)1/(2−κn0​,n​).​
(2)

We always print both indices. The source’s κ1\kappa_1κ1​ means κ1,2\kappa_{1,2}κ1,2​, whereas κ1,n\kappa_{1,n}κ1,n​ compares size nnn with one observation. An adjacent-size comparison κn,n+1\kappa_{n,n+1}κn,n+1​ is different. Here “metric” names a concentration index, not a distance satisfying the axioms of a metric space.

Proposition 1 (Affine invariance and centered-sum growth)

Let XiX_iXi​ be iid real random variables with E∣X1∣<∞\mathbb E|X_1|<\inftyE∣X1​∣<∞, mean μ\muμ, and M(n)=E∣∑i=1nXi−nμ∣M(n)=\mathbb E|\sum_{i=1}^nX_i-n\mu|M(n)=E∣∑i=1n​Xi​−nμ∣. For a∈Ra\in\mathbb Ra∈R and b≠0b\ne0b=0, the deviations for a+bXia+bX_ia+bXi​ equal ∣b∣M(n)|b|M(n)∣b∣M(n); hence every defined κn0,n\kappa_{n_0,n}κn0​,n​ is unchanged. For all integers n≥1n\ge1n≥1, M(n+1)≥M(n)M(n+1)\ge M(n)M(n+1)≥M(n) and M(n)≤nM(1)M(n)\le nM(1)M(n)≤nM(1). If n>1n>1n>1 and M(n)>M(1)>0M(n)>M(1)>0M(n)>M(1)>0, then κ1,n≤1\kappa_{1,n}\le1κ1,n​≤1.

Proof 1

Adding aaa cancels under centering, and multiplying by bbb multiplies absolute deviations by ∣b∣|b|∣b∣, which cancels in their ratio. Conditional Jensen, applied to the independent centered increment Xn+1−μX_{n+1}-\muXn+1​−μ, gives M(n+1)≥M(n)M(n+1)\ge M(n)M(n+1)≥M(n). The triangle inequality gives M(n)≤nM(1)M(n)\le nM(1)M(n)≤nM(1). Under the strict growth assumption, 0<log⁡(M(n)/M(1))≤log⁡n0<\log(M(n)/M(1))\le\log n0<log(M(n)/M(1))≤logn, so the definition gives κ1,n≤1\kappa_{1,n}\le1κ1,n​≤1.

There is no universal lower bound of zero; the examples below show this.

Proposition 2 (Telescoping growth across sample sizes)

Let XiX_iXi​ be iid integrable observations with centered-sum deviations M(n)M(n)M(n). For integers 1≤n0<n1<⋯<nr1\le n_0<n_1<\cdots<n_r1≤n0​<n1​<⋯<nr​, assume M(nj)>M(nj−1)>0M(n_j)>M(n_{j-1})>0M(nj​)>M(nj−1​)>0 for every j=1,…,rj=1,\ldots,rj=1,…,r, so each κnj−1,nj\kappa_{n_{j-1},n_j}κnj−1​,nj​​ is defined. Then

log⁡M(nr)M(n0)=∑j=1rlog⁡(nj/nj−1)2−κnj−1,nj.\begin{aligned} &\log\frac{M(n_r)}{M(n_0)}\\ &\quad=\sum_{j=1}^r \frac{\log(n_j/n_{j-1})}{2-\kappa_{n_{j-1},n_j}}. \end{aligned}​logM(n0​)M(nr​)​=j=1∑r​2−κnj−1​,nj​​log(nj​/nj−1​)​.​
(3)
Proof 2

The definition gives log⁡(M(nj)/M(nj−1))=log⁡(nj/nj−1)/(2−κnj−1,nj)\log(M(n_j)/M(n_{j-1}))=\log(n_j/n_{j-1})/(2-\kappa_{n_{j-1},n_j})log(M(nj​)/M(nj−1​))=log(nj​/nj−1​)/(2−κnj−1​,nj​​). Summing telescopes the logarithms.

This identity does not justify averaging the kappas themselves.

Use kappa_from_mads and stable_kappa to expose the boundaries explicitly:

from xmath.incerto.concentration import kappa_from_mads, stable_kappa

for m0, m in ((1, 2**0.5), (2/3, 14/15), (1, 1), (0, 0), (float("inf"), float("inf"))):
    print(f"MADs {m0:.4g}, {m:.4g}: {kappa_from_mads(m0, m, 2):z.4f}")
for alpha in (1, 1.5, 2):
    print(f"Stable alpha={alpha:g}: {stable_kappa(alpha):.4g}")

Output

MADs 1, 1.414: 0.0000
MADs 0.6667, 0.9333: -0.0600
MADs 1, 1: -inf
MADs 0, 0: nan
MADs inf, inf: nan
Stable alpha=1: nan
Stable alpha=1.5: 0.5
Stable alpha=2: 0

The equal-positive case uses an extended limit. Constant laws and laws without a finite absolute first moment have no kappa under this definition. In particular, a Cauchy law is a limiting benchmark as the stable index decreases to one, not an admissible endpoint.

Stable benchmark and attraction¶

Corollary 1 (Kappa of an integrable stable law)

Let XiX_iXi​ be iid with a nondegenerate stable law of index 1<α≤21<\alpha\le21<α≤2 and mean μ\muμ. For M(n)=E∣Sn−nμ∣M(n)=\mathbb E|S_n-n\mu|M(n)=E∣Sn​−nμ∣,

$$

M(n)=n^{1/\alpha}M(1),\qquad \kappa_{n_0,n}=2-\alpha,\qquad \frac{M(n)}{nM(1)}=n^{1/\alpha-1} $$

for every integer n≥1n\ge1n≥1 and, for kappa, 1≤n0<n1\le n_0<n1≤n0​<n.

Proof 3

Use the stable sum identity, including skew stable laws (Durrett (2019), §3.8, Eq. (3.8.11), p. 189; Taleb (2018), §III.A, Eq. (6), p. 3). Centering by the mean gives Sn−nμ=dn1/α(X1−μ)S_n-n\mu\overset d=n^{1/\alpha}(X_1-\mu)Sn​−nμ=dn1/α(X1​−μ). The law has 0<M(1)<∞0<M(1)<\infty0<M(1)<∞, so taking absolute expectations gives the first formula and strict growth. Substitution in the definition of kappa and division by nM(1)nM(1)nM(1) give the other two.

Skewness does not change the exponent, so it cancels from kappa even though it can change M(1)M(1)M(1). At α=2\alpha=2α=2 the law is Gaussian and kappa is zero. The growth exponent is 1/α1/\alpha1/α; it must not be substituted for α\alphaα in 2−α2-\alpha2−α. The stable-law note fixes the characteristic-function scale and proves the symmetric MAD formula.

Proposition 3 (Kappa under uniformly integrable stable attraction)

Let XiX_iXi​ be iid integrable observations, with mean μ\muμ, Sn=∑i=1nXiS_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_iSn​=∑i=1n​Xi​, M(n)=E∣Sn−nμ∣M(n)=\mathbb E|S_n-n\mu|M(n)=E∣Sn​−nμ∣, and M(1)>0M(1)>0M(1)>0. Suppose an>0a_n>0an​>0, (Sn−nμ)/an(S_n-n\mu)/a_n(Sn​−nμ)/an​ converges in law to a nondegenerate integrable stable variable ZZZ of index 1<α≤21<\alpha\le21<α≤2, the absolute normalized sums are uniformly integrable, and log⁡an/log⁡n→1/α\log a_n/\log n\to1/\alphalogan​/logn→1/α. Then M(n)/an→E∣Z∣M(n)/a_n\to\mathbb E|Z|M(n)/an​→E∣Z∣ and κ1,n→2−α\kappa_{1,n}\to2-\alphaκ1,n​→2−α; this kappa is defined for all sufficiently large nnn.

Proof 4

Convergence in law and uniform integrability give M(n)/an→E∣Z∣∈(0,∞)M(n)/a_n\to\mathbb E|Z|\in(0,\infty)M(n)/an​→E∣Z∣∈(0,∞). Since log⁡an/log⁡n→1/α>0\log a_n/\log n\to1/\alpha>0logan​/logn→1/α>0, an→∞a_n\to\inftyan​→∞ and eventually M(n)>M(1)M(n)>M(1)M(n)>M(1). Also log⁡(M(n)/M(1))/log⁡n→1/α\log(M(n)/M(1))/\log n\to1/\alphalog(M(n)/M(1))/logn→1/α. Substitute in the definition of κ1,n\kappa_{1,n}κ1,n​.

Uniform integrability is what permits convergence of expectations; weak convergence alone does not supply it. This conditional argument does not assert a finite-sample rate for every regularly varying law. A one-sided Pareto and a symmetric Student law with the same tail exponent can have different finite kappas: both their centers and their distribution bodies differ. The numerical comparison below concerns exponent three only.

Student sums and a logarithmic limit¶

Proposition 4 (One- and two-summand Student deviations)

Let XiX_iXi​ be iid Student variables with degrees of freedom ν>1\nu>1ν>1, location zero and scale one, and put M(n)=E∣∑i=1nXi∣M(n)=\mathbb E|\sum_{i=1}^nX_i|M(n)=E∣∑i=1n​Xi​∣. Then

$$

M(1)=\sqrt{\frac\nu\pi}, \frac{\Gamma((\nu-1)/2)}{\Gamma(\nu/2)},\qquad \frac{M(2)}{M(1)}=\sqrt\pi,2^{2-\nu} \frac{\Gamma(\nu-1/2)}{\Gamma(\nu/2)^2}. $$

Proof 5

For completeness, substitute v=1+x2/νv=1+x^2/\nuv=1+x2/ν in 2∫0∞xfν(x) dx2\int_0^\infty x f_\nu(x)\,dx2∫0∞​xfν​(x)dx; the remaining integral is ∫1∞v−(ν+1)/2 dv=2/(ν−1)\int_1^\infty v^{-(\nu+1)/2}\,dv=2/(\nu-1)∫1∞​v−(ν+1)/2dv=2/(ν−1). The gamma recurrence yields the displayed expression.

For two summands, use the Student normal-mixture representation, derived in gamma precision, and represent them as Xi=ν/(2Gi)ZiX_i=\sqrt{\nu/(2G_i)}Z_iXi​=ν/(2Gi​)​Zi​, where the GiG_iGi​ are independent Gamma(ν/2,1)(\nu/2,1)(ν/2,1) and the ZiZ_iZi​ are independent standard normals, independent of the GiG_iGi​. Set T=G1+G2T=G_1+G_2T=G1​+G2​, B=G1/TB=G_1/TB=G1​/T. The change of variables has Jacobian TTT and factorizes the joint density into independent Gamma(ν,1)(\nu,1)(ν,1) and Beta(ν/2,ν/2)(\nu/2,\nu/2)(ν/2,ν/2) densities. Conditional normal absolute moments therefore give

M(2)=ν/π E[T−1/2]×E[(B(1−B))−1/2],M(2)M(1)=π 22−νΓ(ν−1/2)Γ(ν/2)2.\begin{aligned} M(2)&=\sqrt{\nu/\pi}\, \mathbb E[T^{-1/2}]\\ &\quad\times\mathbb E[(B(1-B))^{-1/2}],\\ \frac{M(2)}{M(1)} &=\sqrt\pi\,2^{2-\nu} \frac{\Gamma(\nu-1/2)}{\Gamma(\nu/2)^2}. \end{aligned}M(2)M(1)M(2)​​=ν/π​E[T−1/2]×E[(B(1−B))−1/2],=π​22−νΓ(ν/2)2Γ(ν−1/2)​.​
(4)

The second line follows by the gamma and beta integrals, followed by the gamma duplication identity. These are finite precisely when ν>1\nu>1ν>1.

Locally ν\nuν is also the Student power-tail exponent.

Cubic Student: every integer size¶

Proposition 5 (Cubic Student sums at every integer size)

Let XiX_iXi​ be iid Student variables with degrees of freedom 3, location zero and scale one. Their characteristic function is ϕ(t)=(1+3∣t∣)e−3∣t∣\phi(t)=(1+\sqrt3|t|)e^{-\sqrt3|t|}ϕ(t)=(1+3​∣t∣)e−3​∣t∣. For every integer n≥1n\ge1n≥1, with M(n)=E∣∑i=1nXi∣M(n)=\mathbb E|\sum_{i=1}^nX_i|M(n)=E∣∑i=1n​Xi​∣,

M(n)M(1)=enn1−nΓ(n,n)=n!nn∑j=0n−1njj!,Γ(n,n)=∫n∞tn−1e−t dt.\frac{M(n)}{M(1)}=e^n n^{1-n}\Gamma(n,n) =\frac{n!}{n^n}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{n^j}{j!},\qquad \Gamma(n,n)=\int_n^\infty t^{n-1}e^{-t}\,dt.M(1)M(n)​=enn1−nΓ(n,n)=nnn!​j=0∑n−1​j!nj​,Γ(n,n)=∫n∞​tn−1e−tdt.
(5)

As n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞, M(n)/M(1)∼πn/2M(n)/M(1)\sim\sqrt{\pi n/2}M(n)/M(1)∼πn/2​ and log⁡n κ1,n→2log⁡(π/2)\log n\,\kappa_{1,n}\to2\log(\pi/2)lognκ1,n​→2log(π/2).

Proof 6

At ν=3\nu=3ν=3, the characteristic function is ϕ(t)=(1+3∣t∣)e−3∣t∣\phi(t)=(1+\sqrt3|t|)e^{-\sqrt3|t|}ϕ(t)=(1+3​∣t∣)e−3​∣t∣. One way to verify it is to differentiate the Cauchy Fourier integral ∫Reitx(x2+a2)−1dx=πe−a∣t∣/a\int_{\mathbb R}e^{itx}(x^2+a^2)^{-1}dx=\pi e^{-a|t|}/a∫R​eitx(x2+a2)−1dx=πe−a∣t∣/a with respect to a>0a>0a>0 and use the normalized squared-denominator density at a=3a=\sqrt3a=3​. The Cauchy integral follows by closing the contour in the half-plane where the exponential decays and taking the residue at iaiaia or −ia-ia−ia; the arc integral tends to zero. Differentiation is justified by an integrable bound in a neighborhood of any positive aaa.

We now derive the sum MAD, using the absolute-moment Fourier identity. Integration by parts, then u=3tu=\sqrt3tu=3​t, gives

M(n)=23π n∫0∞(1+u)n−1e−nu du,M(n)M(1)=enn1−nΓ(n,n),Γ(n,n)=∫n∞tn−1e−t dt.\begin{aligned} M(n)&=\frac{2\sqrt3}{\pi}\,n \int_0^\infty(1+u)^{n-1}e^{-nu}\,du,\\ \frac{M(n)}{M(1)} &=e^n n^{1-n}\Gamma(n,n),\\ \Gamma(n,n)&=\int_n^\infty t^{n-1}e^{-t}\,dt. \end{aligned}M(n)M(1)M(n)​Γ(n,n)​=π23​​n∫0∞​(1+u)n−1e−nudu,=enn1−nΓ(n,n),=∫n∞​tn−1e−tdt.​
(6)

The boundary term vanishes at zero because 1−ϕ(t)n=O(t2)1-\phi(t)^n=O(t^2)1−ϕ(t)n=O(t2), and at infinity because the numerator is bounded. The substitution t=n(1+u)t=n(1+u)t=n(1+u) gives the incomplete-gamma expression. This also holds at n=1n=1n=1. Repeated integration by parts yields the independent finite formula

M(n)M(1)=n!nn∑j=0n−1njj!.\frac{M(n)}{M(1)} =\frac{n!}{n^n}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{n^j}{j!}.M(1)M(n)​=nnn!​j=0∑n−1​j!nj​.
(7)

For the limit, e−n∑j<nnj/j!=P(Nn<n)→1/2e^{-n}\sum_{j<n}n^j/j!=P(N_n<n)\to1/2e−n∑j<n​nj/j!=P(Nn​<n)→1/2, where NnN_nNn​ is Poisson with mean nnn. Apply the classical CLT to a sum of nnn independent Poisson(1)(1)(1) variables. Stirling’s formula then gives

M(n)M(1)∼πn/2,log⁡n  κ1,n⟶2log⁡(π/2).\begin{aligned} \frac{M(n)}{M(1)}&\sim\sqrt{\pi n/2},\\ \log n\;\kappa_{1,n}&\longrightarrow2\log(\pi/2). \end{aligned}M(1)M(n)​lognκ1,n​​∼πn/2​,⟶2log(π/2).​
(8)

This constant differs from the one printed in §8.6.1, p. 165. The calculation concerns the kappa anchored at one observation. It is not a bound on the CDF error in a normal approximation, nor on tail-quantile error. It does not prove that a million-term standardized sum is poorly approximated by a Gaussian at every threshold.

What the logarithmic rate measures¶

Proposition 6 (Anchored kappa for finite-variance laws)

Let XiX_iXi​ be iid with mean μ\muμ and variance 0<σ2<∞0<\sigma^2<\infty0<σ2<∞, and set Sn=∑i=1nXiS_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_iSn​=∑i=1n​Xi​, M(n)=E∣Sn−nμ∣M(n)=\mathbb E|S_n-n\mu|M(n)=E∣Sn​−nμ∣. Then M(1)>0M(1)>0M(1)>0, kappa is defined for all sufficiently large nnn, and

M(n)n→σ2/π,log⁡n κ1,n→4log⁡σ2/πM(1).\frac{M(n)}{\sqrt n}\to\sigma\sqrt{2/\pi},\qquad \log n\,\kappa_{1,n}\to 4\log\frac{\sigma\sqrt{2/\pi}}{M(1)}.n​M(n)​→σ2/π​,lognκ1,n​→4logM(1)σ2/π​​.
(9)

In particular, κ1,n→0\kappa_{1,n}\to0κ1,n​→0.

Proof 7

The classical CLT is cited in the limit-law note. The normalized centered sums Yn=(Sn−nμ)/nY_n=(S_n-n\mu)/\sqrt nYn​=(Sn​−nμ)/n​ have second moment σ2\sigma^2σ2; hence E[∣Yn∣1∣Yn∣>K]≤σ2/K\mathbb E[|Y_n|\mathbf1_{|Y_n|>K}]\le\sigma^2/KE[∣Yn​∣1∣Yn​∣>K​]≤σ2/K for K>0K>0K>0. This proves uniform integrability, so

M(n)/n⟶σ2/π,log⁡n  κ1,n⟶4log⁡σ2/πM(1).\begin{aligned} M(n)/\sqrt n&\longrightarrow\sigma\sqrt{2/\pi},\\ \log n\;\kappa_{1,n} &\longrightarrow4\log\frac{\sigma\sqrt{2/\pi}}{M(1)}. \end{aligned}M(n)/n​lognκ1,n​​⟶σ2/π​,⟶4logM(1)σ2/π​​.​
(10)

To obtain the last line, substitute the expansion

log⁡M(n)M(1)=12log⁡n+log⁡σ2/πM(1)+o(1)\begin{aligned} \log\frac{M(n)}{M(1)} &=\tfrac12\log n\\ &\quad+\log\frac{\sigma\sqrt{2/\pi}}{M(1)}+o(1) \end{aligned}logM(1)M(n)​​=21​logn+logM(1)σ2/π​​+o(1)​
(11)

in the definition.

The logarithmic behavior can reflect the mismatch between the one-observation MAD and its Gaussian calibration. If σ2/π=M(1)\sigma\sqrt{2/\pi}=M(1)σ2/π​=M(1), the constant vanishes and this argument gives no nonzero leading rate. Kappa approaching zero does not identify the far tail.

Exponential and gamma sums¶

Proposition 7 (Gamma-sum deviations and the exponential limit)

Let XiX_iXi​ be iid gamma variables with shape r>0r>0r>0 and scale θ>0\theta>0θ>0. For Sn=∑i=1nXiS_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_iSn​=∑i=1n​Xi​ and integer n≥1n\ge1n≥1,

$$

M(n)=\mathbb E|S_n-nr\theta| =\frac{2\theta,(nr)^{nr}e^{-nr}}{\Gamma(nr)}. $$

In the exponential case r=1r=1r=1, log⁡n κ1,n→4−2log⁡(2π)\log n\,\kappa_{1,n}\to4-2\log(2\pi)lognκ1,n​→4−2log(2π).

Proof 8

The gamma convolution identity, proved in the tail catalog, gives SnS_nSn​ shape nrnrnr and scale θ\thetaθ. Use E∣Sn−nrθ∣=2E(Sn−nrθ)+\mathbb E|S_n-nr\theta|=2\mathbb E(S_n-nr\theta)_+E∣Sn​−nrθ∣=2E(Sn​−nrθ)+​. After scaling by θ\thetaθ, the integral is

2θΓ(nr)∫nr∞(t−nr)tnr−1e−t dt.\frac{2\theta}{\Gamma(nr)} \int_{nr}^\infty(t-nr)t^{nr-1}e^{-t}\,dt.Γ(nr)2θ​∫nr∞​(t−nr)tnr−1e−tdt.
(12)

Integration by parts gives Γ(nr+1,nr)=nrΓ(nr,nr)+(nr)nre−nr\Gamma(nr+1,nr)=nr\Gamma(nr,nr)+(nr)^{nr}e^{-nr}Γ(nr+1,nr)=nrΓ(nr,nr)+(nr)nre−nr, which evaluates the integral. At r=1r=1r=1, the parent is exponential with rate 1/θ1/\theta1/θ. Stirling’s formula or the preceding finite-variance argument gives

log⁡n  κ1,n⟶4−2log⁡(2π).\log n\;\kappa_{1,n} \longrightarrow4-2\log(2\pi).lognκ1,n​⟶4−2log(2π).
(13)

Here θ\thetaθ is a local scale, not a natural parameter.

Thus even the exponential law has a positive finite kappa and this logarithmic anchored rate. It still satisfies the Cramér condition and is not subexponential.

Use gaussian_sum_mad, student_sum_mad, gamma_sum_mad, and kappa_from_mads.

from xmath.incerto.concentration import (
    gaussian_sum_mad, student_sum_mad, gamma_sum_mad, kappa_from_mads,
)

for name, mad in (("Gaussian", gaussian_sum_mad), ("Student 3", student_sum_mad), ("Exponential", gamma_sum_mad)):
    for n in (2, 32, 1000):
        print(f"{name}, n={n}: kappa={kappa_from_mads(mad(1), mad(n), n):z.3f}")

Lognormal sums¶

Proposition 8 (A lognormal deviation about its mean)

Let X=eμℓ+σℓZX=e^{\mu_\ell+\sigma_\ell Z}X=eμℓ​+σℓ​Z with Z∼N(0,1)Z\sim N(0,1)Z∼N(0,1), μℓ∈R\mu_\ell\in\mathbb Rμℓ​∈R and σℓ>0\sigma_\ell>0σℓ​>0. Then μ=EX=eμℓ+σℓ2/2\mu=\mathbb EX=e^{\mu_\ell+\sigma_\ell^2/2}μ=EX=eμℓ​+σℓ2​/2, and

$$

M(1)=\mathbb E|X-\mu| =2\mu[2\Phi(\sigma_\ell/2)-1], $$

where Φ\PhiΦ is the standard-normal CDF.

Proof 9

Completing the square gives the mean. Since M(1)=2E(X−μ)+M(1)=2\mathbb E(X-\mu)_+M(1)=2E(X−μ)+​ and X>μX>\muX>μ exactly when Z>σℓ/2Z>\sigma_\ell/2Z>σℓ​/2, exponential tilting shifts the normal mean by σℓ\sigma_\ellσℓ​. Thus E[X1X>μ]=μΦ(σℓ/2)\mathbb E[X\mathbf1_{X>\mu}]=\mu\Phi(\sigma_\ell/2)E[X1X>μ​]=μΦ(σℓ​/2) and P(X>μ)=1−Φ(σℓ/2)P(X>\mu)=1-\Phi(\sigma_\ell/2)P(X>μ)=1−Φ(σℓ​/2), giving the formula.

The parameters are log-location and log-scale, not the mean and standard deviation of XXX.

Sums of independent lognormals are not generally lognormal. Matching a sum’s first two moments to another lognormal gives an approximation, not an identity or a proved bound on kappa.

The mismatch can be checked with third moments. Normalize X←X/μX\leftarrow X/\muX←X/μ. Through the numerical calculation below, XXX denotes the mean-one variable eσℓZ−σℓ2/2e^{\sigma_\ell Z-\sigma_\ell^2/2}eσℓ​Z−σℓ2​/2, XiX_iXi​ are independent copies, and SnS_nSn​ is their sum. We retain μ\muμ as the original mean, so M(n)=μE∣Sn−n∣M(n)=\mu\mathbb E|S_n-n|M(n)=μE∣Sn​−n∣ restores the original units. This positive rescaling preserves skewness and kappa.

Proposition 9 (A lognormal fit cannot be the exact sum law)

Let Xi=eσℓZi−σℓ2/2X_i=e^{\sigma_\ell Z_i-\sigma_\ell^2/2}Xi​=eσℓ​Zi​−σℓ2​/2 for iid standard normals ZiZ_iZi​, with σℓ>0\sigma_\ell>0σℓ​>0, and set v=eσℓ2−1v=e^{\sigma_\ell^2}-1v=eσℓ2​−1. For any integer n>1n>1n>1, the average Xˉn\bar X_nXˉn​ and the lognormal law with its same mean and variance have respective skewnesses

(v+3)v/nand(v/n+3)v/n.(v+3)\sqrt{v/n}\quad\text{and}\quad(v/n+3)\sqrt{v/n}.(v+3)v/n​and(v/n+3)v/n​.
(14)

They differ, so neither the average nor the sum is lognormal.

Proof 10

Write v=Var⁡(X)=eσℓ2−1>0v=\operatorname{Var}(X)=e^{\sigma_\ell^2}-1>0v=Var(X)=eσℓ2​−1>0. The moments EXj=ej(j−1)σℓ2/2\mathbb EX^j=e^{j(j-1)\sigma_\ell^2/2}EXj=ej(j−1)σℓ2​/2 give third centered moment v2(v+3)v^2(v+3)v2(v+3). Independence makes the variance of the average v/nv/nv/n and its third centered moment v2(v+3)/n2v^2(v+3)/n^2v2(v+3)/n2. The skewnesses of the actual average and a moment-matched lognormal are therefore

skew⁡(Xˉn)=(v+3)v/n,skew⁡(fitted lognormal)=(v/n+3)v/n.\begin{aligned} \operatorname{skew}(\bar X_n)&=(v+3)\sqrt{v/n},\\ \operatorname{skew}(\text{fitted lognormal})&=(v/n+3)\sqrt{v/n}. \end{aligned}skew(Xˉn​)skew(fitted lognormal)​=(v+3)v/n​,=(v/n+3)v/n​.​
(15)

Their difference is v(1−1/n)v/n>0v(1-1/n)\sqrt{v/n}>0v(1−1/n)v/n​>0. If the average were lognormal, its first two moments would determine exactly the fitted lognormal. Positive scaling transfers the obstruction to the sum.

This does not quantify the lognormal approximation error.

We prove the three limits at the scope used in §8.6.2, pp. 166–168.

Corollary 2 (Fixed log-scale and increasing sample size)

For iid lognormal Xi=eμℓ+σℓZiX_i=e^{\mu_\ell+\sigma_\ell Z_i}Xi​=eμℓ​+σℓ​Zi​ with fixed μℓ∈R\mu_\ell\in\mathbb Rμℓ​∈R, σℓ>0\sigma_\ell>0σℓ​>0 and iid standard normals ZiZ_iZi​, the centered-sum index satisfies κ1,n→0\kappa_{1,n}\to0κ1,n​→0 as n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞.

Proof 11

The lognormal law has positive finite variance. Apply Proposition 6.

Proposition 10 (Fixed sample size and vanishing log-scale)

Fix an integer n>1n>1n>1 and μℓ∈R\mu_\ell\in\mathbb Rμℓ​∈R. For iid Xi=eμℓ+σℓZiX_i=e^{\mu_\ell+\sigma_\ell Z_i}Xi​=eμℓ​+σℓ​Zi​ with standard-normal ZiZ_iZi​ and σℓ>0\sigma_\ell>0σℓ​>0, M(n)/M(1)→nM(n)/M(1)\to\sqrt nM(n)/M(1)→n​ and κ1,n→0\kappa_{1,n}\to0κ1,n​→0 as σℓ↓0\sigma_\ell\downarrow0σℓ​↓0.

Proof 12

By Proposition 1, dividing each summand by its mean preserves the MAD ratio and kappa. In this proof, write X=eσℓZ−σℓ2/2X=e^{\sigma_\ell Z-\sigma_\ell^2/2}X=eσℓ​Z−σℓ2​/2 for a normalized summand. As σℓ↓0\sigma_\ell\downarrow0σℓ​↓0,

E[(X−1σℓ−Z)2]=eσℓ2−1σℓ2−1⟶0.\begin{aligned} \mathbb E\left[\left(\frac{X-1}{\sigma_\ell}-Z\right)^2\right] &=\frac{e^{\sigma_\ell^2}-1}{\sigma_\ell^2}-1\\ &\longrightarrow0. \end{aligned}E[(σℓ​X−1​−Z)2]​=σℓ2​eσℓ2​−1​−1⟶0.​
(16)

This identity follows from EX2=eσℓ2\mathbb EX^2=e^{\sigma_\ell^2}EX2=eσℓ2​ and E[ZX]=σℓ\mathbb E[ZX]=\sigma_\ellE[ZX]=σℓ​. A finite sum preserves L2L^2L2 convergence, which implies convergence of absolute expectations. Thus the MAD ratio tends to n\sqrt nn​, and kappa tends to zero.

Proposition 11 (Fixed sample size and increasing log-scale)

Fix an integer n>1n>1n>1 and μℓ∈R\mu_\ell\in\mathbb Rμℓ​∈R. For iid Xi=eμℓ+σℓZiX_i=e^{\mu_\ell+\sigma_\ell Z_i}Xi​=eμℓ​+σℓ​Zi​ with standard-normal ZiZ_iZi​, M(n)/M(1)→nM(n)/M(1)\to nM(n)/M(1)→n and κ1,n→1\kappa_{1,n}\to1κ1,n​→1 as σℓ→∞\sigma_\ell\to\inftyσℓ​→∞.

Proof 13

Again use Proposition 1 to divide each summand by its mean, and write XiX_iXi​ for the normalized summands within this proof. As σℓ→∞\sigma_\ell\to\inftyσℓ​→∞, couple a fixed finite set of normal variables. Each Xi=eσℓZi−σℓ2/2→0X_i=e^{\sigma_\ell Z_i-\sigma_\ell^2/2}\to0Xi​=eσℓ​Zi​−σℓ2​/2→0 almost surely, although its mean remains one. For their sum SnS_nSn​,

E∣Sn−n∣=2n−2Emin⁡(Sn,n),Emin⁡(Sn,n)⟶0.\begin{aligned} &\mathbb E|S_n-n|\\ &\quad=2n-2\mathbb E\min(S_n,n),\\ &\mathbb E\min(S_n,n)\longrightarrow0. \end{aligned}​E∣Sn​−n∣=2n−2Emin(Sn​,n),Emin(Sn​,n)⟶0.​
(17)

The last line is bounded convergence. Therefore M(n)/M(1)→nM(n)/M(1)\to nM(n)/M(1)→n and κ1,n→1\kappa_{1,n}\to1κ1,n​→1.

The order of limits matters. Every fixed lognormal law still has all power moments and belongs to the Gaussian domain of attraction.

A bounded numerical calculation¶

Proposition 12 (A bounded conditional payoff for lognormal MAD)

Let Xi=eσℓZi−σℓ2/2X_i=e^{\sigma_\ell Z_i-\sigma_\ell^2/2}Xi​=eσℓ​Zi​−σℓ2​/2 for iid standard normals ZiZ_iZi​, σℓ>0\sigma_\ell>0σℓ​>0, and integer n≥1n\ge1n≥1. Set Sn=∑i=1nXiS_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_iSn​=∑i=1n​Xi​ and a=n−∑i<nXia=n-\sum_{i<n}X_ia=n−∑i<n​Xi​. For any original mean μ>0\mu>0μ>0, the centered-sum MAD of the summands μXi\mu X_iμXi​ is M(n)=2μE(n−Sn)+M(n)=2\mu\mathbb E(n-S_n)_+M(n)=2μE(n−Sn​)+​. The conditional expectation of (n−Sn)+(n-S_n)_+(n−Sn​)+​ given X1,…,Xn−1X_1,\ldots,X_{n-1}X1​,…,Xn−1​ is zero when a≤0a\le0a≤0 and, when a>0a>0a>0, equals

E[(a−Xn)+∣a]=aΦ ⁣(log⁡aσℓ+σℓ2)−Φ ⁣(log⁡aσℓ−σℓ2).\begin{aligned} \mathbb E[(a-X_n)_+\mid a] &=a\Phi\!\left(\frac{\log a}{\sigma_\ell}+\frac{\sigma_\ell}{2}\right)\\ &\quad-\Phi\!\left(\frac{\log a}{\sigma_\ell}-\frac{\sigma_\ell}{2}\right). \end{aligned}E[(a−Xn​)+​∣a]​=aΦ(σℓ​loga​+2σℓ​​)−Φ(σℓ​loga​−2σℓ​​).​
(18)

This conditional payoff lies in [0,n][0,n][0,n].

Proof 14

An integrable centered variable has equal positive- and negative-part expectations. Since ESn=n\mathbb ES_n=nESn​=n, this gives E∣Sn−n∣=2E(n−Sn)+\mathbb E|S_n-n|=2\mathbb E(n-S_n)_+E∣Sn​−n∣=2E(n−Sn​)+​. Conditional independence reduces the payoff to E(a−Xn)+\mathbb E(a-X_n)_+E(a−Xn​)+​. For a>0a>0a>0, split it as aP(Xn<a)−E[Xn1Xn<a]aP(X_n<a)-\mathbb E[X_n\mathbf1_{X_n<a}]aP(Xn​<a)−E[Xn​1Xn​<a​]. Completing the square gives the two normal CDF terms. Nonnegativity and a≤na\le na≤n give the bound; for a≤0a\le0a≤0 the payoff is zero.

Here the expectation integrates over XnX_nXn​ with the first n−1n-1n−1 summands fixed. The simulated payoff lies between zero and nnn. Multiplying its sample average by 2μ2\mu2μ estimates M(n)M(n)M(n) without estimating an unbounded upper-tail payoff. This uses a known model mean. It is not available merely because a dataset contains only small observations.

Use lognormal_sum_mad. Its mu and sigma arguments are μℓ\mu_\ellμℓ​ and σℓ\sigma_\ellσℓ​; the example uses μℓ=0\mu_\ell=0μℓ​=0, so the original mean is μ=eσℓ2/2\mu=e^{\sigma_\ell^2/2}μ=eσℓ2​/2. The standard error below describes Monte Carlo integration, not uncertainty about the assumed lognormal law.

from xmath.incerto.concentration import lognormal_sum_mad, kappa_from_mads

for sigma in (0.5, 1, 2):
    single = lognormal_sum_mad(1, sigma)["mad"]
    result = lognormal_sum_mad(8, sigma, random_state=20261088)
    kappa = kappa_from_mads(single, result["mad"], 8)
    print(f"sigma={sigma:g}: MAD={result['mad']:.3f}, MC SE={result['mc_se']:.3f}, kappa={kappa:.3f}")

Output

sigma=0.5: MAD=1.343, MC SE=0.011, kappa=0.108
sigma=1: MAD=4.413, MC SE=0.032, kappa=0.338
sigma=2: MAD=50.405, MC SE=0.254, kappa=0.707

Negative kappa needs no bimodality¶

Proposition 13 (A unimodal law with negative kappa)

Let XiX_iXi​ be iid with symmetric triangular density f(x)=(2−∣x∣)/4f(x)=(2-|x|)/4f(x)=(2−∣x∣)/4 on [−2,2][-2,2][−2,2], zero elsewhere. This density has a single mode at zero, and for M(n)=E∣∑i=1nXi∣M(n)=\mathbb E|\sum_{i=1}^nX_i|M(n)=E∣∑i=1n​Xi​∣,

$$

M(1)=2/3,\qquad M(2)=14/15,\qquad \kappa_{1,2}=2-\frac{\log2}{\log(7/5)}<0. $$

Proof 15

Consider the symmetric triangular density f(x)=(2−∣x∣)/4f(x)=(2-|x|)/4f(x)=(2−∣x∣)/4 on [−2,2][-2,2][−2,2]. It has a single mode at zero and can be written as the sum of two independent Uniform[−1,1][-1,1][−1,1] variables. Direct integration gives M(1)=2/3M(1)=2/3M(1)=2/3. The sum of two copies is a sum of four such uniforms and has M(2)=14/15M(2)=14/15M(2)=14/15. Here is an explicit calculation of the second value. If TTT is a sum of four Uniform[0,1][0,1][0,1] variables, symmetry and integration of its CDF give

E∣2T−4∣=4∫02P(T<t) dt,P(T<t)=t4−4(t−1)+424,0≤t≤2,E∣2T−4∣=4(32−4)120=1415.\begin{aligned} \mathbb E|2T-4| &=4\int_0^2P(T<t)\,dt,\\ P(T<t)&=\frac{t^4-4(t-1)_+^4}{24},\\ &\hspace{2em}0\le t\le2,\\ \mathbb E|2T-4|&=\frac{4(32-4)}{120}=\frac{14}{15}. \end{aligned}E∣2T−4∣P(T<t)E∣2T−4∣​=4∫02​P(T<t)dt,=24t4−4(t−1)+4​​,0≤t≤2,=1204(32−4)​=1514​.​
(19)

The CDF formula is inclusion–exclusion for the volume below u1+⋯+u4<tu_1+\cdots+u_4<tu1​+⋯+u4​<t in the unit cube. Thus

κ1,2=2−log⁡2log⁡(7/5)<0.\kappa_{1,2}=2-\frac{\log2}{\log(7/5)}<0.κ1,2​=2−log(7/5)log2​<0.
(20)

This counterexample corrects the bimodality suggestion in §8.4.4, p. 162. Negative kappa says only that this MAD grows more slowly than the Gaussian benchmark across the chosen sizes.

The source’s separated Gaussian mixture supplies another example.

Proposition 14 (Gaussian location mixtures have no finite kappa lower bound)

Let XiX_iXi​ be iid copies of aR+σZaR+\sigma ZaR+σZ, with a∈Ra\in\mathbb Ra∈R, σ>0\sigma>0σ>0, equiprobable R∈{−1,1}R\in\{-1,1\}R∈{−1,1} and independent Z∼N(0,1)Z\sim N(0,1)Z∼N(0,1). For b∈Rb\in\mathbb Rb∈R, s>0s>0s>0, define

$$

H(b,s)=s\sqrt{2/\pi}e^{-b^2/(2s^2)} +|b|[2\Phi(|b|/s)-1]. $$

Then H(b,s)=E∣b+sZ∣H(b,s)=\mathbb E|b+sZ|H(b,s)=E∣b+sZ∣ and, for integer n≥1n\ge1n≥1,

$$

M(n)=\mathbb E\left|\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right| =\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk2^{-n}H(a(2k-n),\sigma\sqrt n). $$

In particular, M(1)=H(a,σ)M(1)=H(a,\sigma)M(1)=H(a,σ) and M(2)={H(2a,2σ)+H(0,2σ)}/2M(2)=\{H(2a,\sqrt2\sigma)+H(0,\sqrt2\sigma)\}/2M(2)={H(2a,2​σ)+H(0,2​σ)}/2. For fixed σ>0\sigma>0σ>0, κ1,2→−∞\kappa_{1,2}\to-\inftyκ1,2​→−∞ as a→∞a\to\inftya→∞.

Proof 16

Condition on the number KKK of positive signs:

K∼Binomial⁡(n,1/2),Sn∣K∼N(a(2K−n),nσ2).\begin{aligned} K&\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,1/2),\\ S_n\mid K&\sim N(a(2K-n),n\sigma^2). \end{aligned}KSn​∣K​∼Binomial(n,1/2),∼N(a(2K−n),nσ2).​
(21)

For b∈Rb\in\mathbb Rb∈R and s>0s>0s>0, let H(b,s)=E∣b+sZ∣H(b,s)=\mathbb E|b+sZ|H(b,s)=E∣b+sZ∣. Splitting the normal integral at −b/s-b/s−b/s gives

H(b,s)=s2/π e−b2/(2s2)+∣b∣[2Φ(∣b∣/s)−1],M(n)=∑k=0n(nk)2−n×H(a(2k−n),σn).\begin{aligned} H(b,s)&=s\sqrt{2/\pi}\,e^{-b^2/(2s^2)}\\ &\quad+|b|[2\Phi(|b|/s)-1],\\ M(n)&=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk2^{-n}\\ &\quad\times H(a(2k-n),\sigma\sqrt n). \end{aligned}H(b,s)M(n)​=s2/π​e−b2/(2s2)+∣b∣[2Φ(∣b∣/s)−1],=k=0∑n​(kn​)2−n×H(a(2k−n),σn​).​
(22)

For fixed s>0s>0s>0, H(b,s)/b→1H(b,s)/b\to1H(b,s)/b→1 as b→+∞b\to+\inftyb→+∞. Thus M(2)/M(1)→1M(2)/M(1)\to1M(2)/M(1)→1. The ratio is strictly greater than one: conditional on any first summand, adding the independent Gaussian-mixture increment gives both signs positive probability, so Jensen’s absolute-value inequality is strict. Consequently the positive denominator log⁡(M(2)/M(1))\log(M(2)/M(1))log(M(2)/M(1)) tends to zero and kappa tends to −∞-\infty−∞.

This finite mixture calculation underlies the figure.

Use normal_location_mixture_sum_mad.

from xmath.incerto.concentration import normal_location_mixture_sum_mad, kappa_from_mads

for a in (0, 1, 3):
    m1 = normal_location_mixture_sum_mad(1, a)
    m2 = normal_location_mixture_sum_mad(2, a)
    print(f"separation={a:g}: kappa={kappa_from_mads(m1, m2, 2):.3f}")

Output

separation=0: kappa=0.000
separation=1: kappa=-0.134
separation=3: kappa=-2.028

Reproduce and continue¶

uv run python demos/incerto/concentration.py regenerates these figures and the sample-sufficiency figure. All curves are population calculations or explicitly labeled simulations. The sample-size calculation uses absolute error, not a universal threshold for confidence-interval validity.

Source locators: Taleb (2025), ch. 8, §§8.2–8.4, pp. 156–162, and §§8.6.1–8.6.4, pp. 164–169. The attached paper Taleb (2018) contains the earlier definition and derivations in §§II–IV and appendices D–G. The proofs, counterexample, computations and figures here are original treatments of that scope.
